body_markdown: This is a strong example of where AI for science is moving beyond molecule generation into synthesis planning. RetroChimera is especially interesting because it combines two complementary approaches: a flexible de novo model and a more constrained template-based model, then learns how to rank their proposals. That helps reduce some of the trade-off between novelty and reliability. One question may become increasingly important as systems like this move toward closed-loop laboratory workflows: when does a predicted route become an execution-ready route? A synthesis proposal may look chemically plausible, yet execution still depends on reagent availability, reaction conditions, equipment state, safety constraints, intermediate verification, and whether previous steps actually succeeded. So the next frontier may not only be better retrosynthesis prediction, but connecting prediction to a verifiable state-transition process in which each experimental step is checked before the next one is authorized. That could be an important bridge from “AI suggests chemistry” to “AI participates safely and reproducibly in chemistry.”
